scenes.narration: Every QR code has three big corner squares. So why *three*?

scenes.visual: illustration over the shoulder of a relaxed hand holding a smartphone, its camera pointed at a plain QR code card on a wooden cafe table, the phone screen showing a blurry cloud of tiny dark dots with three small squares at its corners glowing bright warm orange as the brightest thing in the frame, phone and card big in the middle of the frame between 30 and 65 percent of the height, simple cool blue background, no text, no logos, no brand
scenes.narration: To your camera, it's a mess of dots. The squares show it *where* to look... and that empty corner? A *clue*.
scenes.headline: WHERE'S THE *CODE*?

scenes.visual: 2D animation: one big QR corner square on a white card; an orange scan line sweeps through its middle and each dark and light run lights up, the readout counting 1 . 1 . 3 . 1 . 1, then THE BEAT
scenes.narration: Draw a line through one: dark, light, *thick* dark, light, dark. One, one, three, one, one. Like a drum beat.
scenes.headline: STEP 1/3: A *BEAT*

scenes.visual: illustration of a messy stack of open magazines and newspapers on a simple desk, a relaxed hand holding a big magnifying glass over one page, the magnifying glass rim bright warm orange as the brightest thing in the frame, pages showing only soft grey blocks and abstract shapes, everything big in the middle of the frame between 30 and 65 percent of the height, plain cool blue background, no readable text, no logos, no people's faces

scenes.headline: STEP 2/3: *NEVER* SEEN

youtube.title: Why do QR codes have three squares? #shorts
youtube.description:
Why do QR codes have three squares? Those big QR code corner squares are called finder patterns. Draw a line through one and you get dark, light, thick dark, light, dark: a 1:1:3:1:1 rhythm that almost never turns up in printed pictures or text, so your camera can find the code fast. And because there are only three, they make an L: the empty fourth corner tells your phone which way is up, so it reads from any angle, even upside down. QR codes were made in 1994 by a Denso Wave team led by Masahiro Hara to track car parts.
